newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seeks family tax cut, closes loopholes.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seeks family tax cut, closes loopholes.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Thursday proposed to give taxpayers a $98 billion tax cut over the next five years to help middle-class families with children, promote higher education and encourage savings.

In his formal budget request for the coming 1998 fiscal year, the president said the tax cuts would be paid for partially by trimming unwarranted corporate tax subsidies and extending other taxes for a total of $76 billion.

The plan would produce a net tax cut of $24 billion for taxpayers on an expected $8.6 trillion of total individual and corporate taxes and other income to the government -- less than three tenths of one percent over the five years.
Most of these tax cuts would be repealed if the economy failed to perform as the White House expected and more taxes were needed to bring the budget into balance.
Separately, the government would raise $36 billion over five years by selling off the rights to parts of the airwaves.
The tax proposals were largely expected by the Republican-controlled Congress, which hopes to negotiate broader tax relief, including a deep reduction in capital gains tax paid on investment profits.
They have some reason for hope since Clinton has said he is not as tied to capital gains taxes as other Democrats.

His most expensive tax proposal would cost $46 billion and give families a $500 tax credit for children under age 13 -- an amount they could take off their final tax bill each April. But the credit would be only $300 in 1997 and would reach $500 only in 2002. It would be phased out for those with taxable incomes above $60,000.

Families with children headed to college would see a $1,500 tax credit for new HOPE scholarships for the first two years. A new deduction for college or post-secondary training would be available to all, valued at $5,000 per family in 1997 and 1998 and $10,000 per family in 1999 and beyond.

It would not be available to families with taxable income over $100,000 a year. Currently, education is deductible if it is job-related. These two education proposals would save taxpayers $36.1 billion over the five years.

Clinton's capital gains tax relief centres on a relatively small tax break for homeowners, raising the amount of profit that can be excluded from taxation upon resale. It would mainly expand current tax breaks available to homeowners over age 55 who move to smaller homes and would be worth $1.5 billion over five years. The exclusion could be used every two years rather than once a lifetime as at present. Now, people under age 55 face no tax bill if they roll profits on home sales into higher-priced homes.

To expand personal savings, income limits on contributions to deductible Individual Retirement Accounts would be doubled to a maximum of $100,000 taxable income from $50,000. The president also proposed a new Special IRA where contributions would not be tax deductible but interest would accumulate tax free if held five years.
Both types of IRA could be tapped to fund higher education, first-time home purchases or expenses when unemployment checks run out. This would be worth $5.5 billion to taxpayers over the five years.

As part of his welfare reform package, Clinton asked Congress to give companies tax credits worth $5,000 per employee aimed to move people from welfare to work. And, he called for $1 billion in tax incentives over five years to help economically distressed urban areas.
Several controversial tax breaks for investors would be tightened or closed by his proposal.

Investors, particularly those holding mutual funds, would be forced to use the average price of a stock when figuring gains or losses upon sale, called "average cost basis." Currently investors have more flexibility in calculating for tax purposes the sale price of their stocks.

Another profitable tax break for investors, called "selling short against the box," would be eliminated in Clinton's plan. Rather than selling stock that is owned, investors are able to sell identical stock they have borrowed with their own stock used as collateral.

One important tax renewal cleared the tax-writing Senate Finance Committee on Wednesday. The panel approved an emergency extension of the 10 percent airline ticket tax that had expired in December. The White House said it plans to propose replacing this tax with a fee on services provided by the Federal Aviation Administration.
